name: PT Bangun Kosambi Sukses Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bangun Kosambi Sukses: a township premium on a raw-land seller
frontmatter.summary: We initiate CBDK at SELL with a target of Rp1,582, a return of -44.3% against the Rp2,900 price. The market pays more than our undiscounted RNAV for a land bank whose monetisation depends on plot sales running at a fraction of revenue, and at a P/BV far above the sector median.
thesis: The shares trade above the undiscounted RNAV of the land bank and income assets; our RNAV method, before the property discount, already sits below the market price, so the SELL does not depend on a bearish view of plot prices.

The profit and loss account is running on a customer-advance book, not on current sales: FY2025 revenue of IDR2,503.6bn compares with marketing sales of IDR430.2bn, so the revenue base must normalise as the backlog unwinds.
At 1.5x P/BV on the 30 June 2026 book against a peer median of 0.7x, the market capitalises a township option that the company has not yet converted into a repeatable sales run-rate.

Downside is cushioned by a net-cash balance sheet, a controlling shareholder with every incentive to keep the township funded, and a recurring-income base (NICE, the Hilton under construction) that we value at a cap rate.
The main upside risk is that a single bulk commercial land transaction, like the one that lifted FY2024 marketing sales, re-rates the whole equity; we treat that as the bull case, not the base case.

catalysts.event: Hilton PIK Dua, the five-star hotel under construction, is targeted to open in the second half of 2027, adding recurring income
FY2026 audited results and the FY2026 dividend decision at the annual meeting
Full-year marketing sales against the company target of {{fact.F10|money}}
Any decision on a further bulk commercial land sale or a township asset monetisation

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bangun Kosambi Sukses at **SELL** with a twelve-month target of **Rp1,582**, which implies a total return of **-44.3%** from the Rp2,900 price. The target is built from three methods: RNAV at 60% weight, P/E at 20% and P/BV at 20%, rolled forward one year at our cost of equity of 11.9% and net of the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp35. The probability-weighted scenario value is Rp1,582, with no liquidity discount applied. [S0]

The core of the call is simple. CBDK owns and is developing a township in the Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua area of Tangerang, with a land bank of 702 ha at the last annual report date and a book of customer advances of IDR9,546.8bn [S3]. Our RNAV build values the land at Rp927 per share after a 40.0% discount to appraised value; the market price of Rp2,900 is above that, and above the undiscounted RNAV per share that the model computes. In other words, the equity is priced as if the option value of the township were already realised, with no discount for the years of plot sales still required to convert land into cash. [S0, S3]

The variant view is about the sales run-rate rather than the asset. Marketing sales were IDR430.2bn in FY2025 against a target the company set at a higher figure, and IDR448.0bn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S3, S2]. Reported revenue of IDR2,503.6bn is therefore being recognised out of the advance book, not out of current demand: the company sold plots in earlier periods, collected the cash, and is handing them over now [S3]. That is a legitimate business model, but it means the profit and loss account flatters the underlying sales momentum, and it means revenue has to step down once the backlog is consumed unless a new bulk transaction lands. [S3, S4]

What would move the value: a large commercial land sale to an institutional or corporate buyer, an independent appraisal of the land bank that supports a higher value than the audited inventory book, faster conversion at NICE and the Hilton, or a lower rate path that revives plot demand. Against that, the balance sheet is in net cash, there is no meaningful foreign-currency debt, and the controlling shareholder has funded the township through its own master plan, so the downside is a de-rating rather than a solvency event. [S3, S0]

CBDK is a property developer focused on the Central Business District of the Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua township in Tangerang, Banten, on the northern coast of Greater Jakarta. The company listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange in January 2025 and is controlled by PT Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua Tbk, itself part of the Agung Sedayu and Salim group sphere, which together hold a large majority of the shares [S3, S4]. The business is best understood as a township land monetisation story with a small and growing recurring-income arm, rather than as a conventional residential developer with a broad product pipeline. [S3]

The development segment is the whole of the economics today. In FY2025, development revenue was IDR2,420.6bn out of total revenue of IDR2,503.6bn, while rental and other recurring revenue was IDR35.5bn [S3]. Within development, commercial land plots dominate: they contributed the large majority of the first nine months of FY2026 revenue, with commercial products such as SOHO The Bund, Bizpark and Rukan Pasar Milenial and residential products such as Rumah Milenial and Permata Hijau Residence making up the balance [S4, S2]. The sale of raw or semi-finished plots carries almost no construction cost, which is why the group gross margin reaches 66.0% and the EBITDA margin 57.5%. [S3, S0]

The land bank is the asset that matters. The company reports 702 ha of land reserves, most of it inside the township, carried on two balance-sheet lines that together total IDR6,909.5bn of current inventory and IDR6,910.8bn of undeveloped land at the last audited date [S3 p.393-394]. The strategy is to accelerate the use of productive land, continue building township infrastructure, and add commercial and residential products that fit the demand it sees from businesses wanting an address in the district [S3]. That strategy is capital-light in the development segment because buyers prepay: customer advances stood at IDR9,546.8bn at the end of FY2025, which funds infrastructure without bank debt. [S3]

The recurring-income arm is small but strategically important. CBDK owns the Nusantara International Convention Exhibition, or NICE, acquired in January 2025 with proceeds from the listing, and describes it as the largest convention and exhibition centre in Jakarta and its surroundings [S3]. NICE has hosted a steady calendar of events including the Java Jazz Festival and Hyrox, and the company is building the Hilton PIK Dua, a five-star hotel targeted to open in the second half of 2027 [S2]. Rental revenue of IDR35.5bn is still trivial against the development line, but it is the part of the business that could eventually cover fixed costs through a property downcycle. [S3]

On competitive position, CBDK is not a volume leader among Indonesian developers. It is a township specialist with a single master plan, competing for corporate and retail buyers against other Greater Jakarta satellite townships and against the broader estate of its parent. Its advantage is location and infrastructure: the partial opening of the KATARAJA toll road section that connects the area to Soekarno-Hatta airport and the wider Jabodetabek network has improved access, and third-party facilities such as bank buildings and the Beachwalk lifestyle centre have made the district more usable [S2]. Its disadvantage is concentration: one township, one controlling shareholder, and a land supply that comes from the master plan of the parent. [S3, S2]

The group structure is straightforward but concentrated. PT Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua is the controlling shareholder with a stake above four-fifths of the shares, the public holds the remainder, and the President Commissioner, Richard Halim Kusuma, is disclosed as the ultimate beneficial owner [S3]. The President Director is Steven Kusumo [S2]. The group employs 167.0 people directly, which underlines how much of the development work is contracted out and how small the fixed cost base is. [S0]

The Indonesian property market entered 2026 in a gradual recovery rather than a boom. The review of the company describes national residential sales rising slightly year on year in 2025 but accelerating sharply on a quarterly basis in the final quarter, citing Bank Indonesia data, and points to government incentives, easier permitting and middle-class purchasing power as the policy supports for the sector [S3]. Gross domestic product growth remained in the mid single digits, household consumption was solid, and the rupiah and interest rates were described as stable [S3]. For a developer selling commercial plots to businesses, that backdrop is supportive but not transformative: demand tracks business formation and confidence more than it tracks household mortgage rates. [S3]

The macro driver that matters most for CBDK is the interest-rate path, because it sets both the cost of funding for the buyer and the capitalisation rate applied to the recurring assets. Our macro deck carries Bank Indonesia policy at 5.8 rate at the long end and inflation near 3.3 rate, with real growth around 5.3 rate; we use a cost of equity of 11.9% and a cap rate of 8.5% for the income assets [S0]. The company itself lists global geopolitical tension, rupiah volatility, inflation and interest rates as the external risks it monitors, which is consistent with a business whose buyers are small and medium enterprises with financing needs. [S3, S2]

Regulation cuts two ways. On the supportive side, the government agenda of incentives and easier permitting for housing and property is explicitly cited by the company as a growth driver, and a VAT exemption or a continuation of the non-collected VAT treatment for housing would help demand for plots and products [S3]. On the constraining side, the affiliated-transaction regime under the capital-market rules governs how the company buys land and services from its parent, and the annual report devotes a section to compliance with those rules [S3]. For an investor, the practical question is not whether the rules exist but whether the land transfer pricing between the parent and the listed entity is fair; the company states that all related-party agreements were prepared independently and on arm's-length terms, and we have no evidence to the contrary. [S3]

Demand for the specific product CBDK sells is narrower than headline residential statistics suggest. Commercial land plots in a master-planned district are bought by businesses that want a branded address, by investors anticipating further infrastructure, and by operators who will build on the plot. That demand is lumpy and relationship-driven: the FY2024 marketing sales figure of IDR2,120.0bn against IDR430.2bn in FY2025 shows how one or two large transactions can dominate a year [S5, S3]. The first nine months of FY2026, at IDR448.0bn, were up strongly on the prior year but still small relative to the revenue being recognised, which tells us the bulk market has not yet returned. [S2]

On the five forces, buyer power is high because corporate plot buyers are few and can wait; supplier power is high because the land comes from the master plan of the controlling shareholder rather than an open market; the threat of substitutes is meaningful because Greater Jakarta has several competing satellite townships and office districts; rivalry is moderate because each township is differentiated by location and infrastructure; and the threat of new entrants is low at the township scale, since assembling and permitting a comparable land position takes years. The moat, in other words, is the land position and the infrastructure already sunk into it, not the brand or the sales machine. [S3, S2]

The competitive landscape is best framed by the parent. Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua is itself listed and trades at a premium P/BV to the developer sector, reflecting the appetite of the market for the township story rather than for its reported earnings [S0]. CBDK is the CBD arm of that township, which gives it a reflected premium and a reflected dependency: the master plan of the parent determines access, amenities and the sequencing of land release, and the capital needs of the parent can influence how the listed subsidiary is run. That is a structural feature of the investment case, not a temporary one. [S3, S0]

External influences beyond rates are limited but not absent. The company has no material foreign-currency debt, so rupiah moves affect buyer sentiment rather than the balance sheet [S0]. Commodity input costs matter less than for a builder because the product is land, and construction of township infrastructure is contracted. The main external swing factor is therefore confidence: a recession that freezes corporate plot purchases would hit marketing sales before it hit reported revenue, because revenue is protected by the advance book for a period. [S3]

The reported history is one of rapid growth in revenue and profit, driven by land handovers. Revenue rose from IDR1,953.5bn in FY2023 to IDR2,249.0bn in FY2024 and IDR2,503.6bn in FY2025, with gross profit of IDR1,653.6bn and EBITDA of IDR1,438.4bn in the last year [S0, S3]. Net profit attributable to owners was IDR578.5bn, IDR924.8bn and IDR1,360.0bn across the three years, and earnings per share reached Rp240 in FY2025 [S0]. The margins are extraordinary by developer standards, with a gross margin of 66.0%, an EBITDA margin of 57.5% and a net margin of 54.3%, and they are explained by the product: land plots sold with little or no construction cost attached. [S0, S3]

Our forecast continues the growth but at a decelerating rate. We model revenue of IDR2,855.5bn in FY2026, IDR3,215.4bn in FY2027 and IDR3,441.7bn in FY2028, with EBITDA of IDR2,026.4bn, IDR2,185.2bn and IDR2,236.3bn and attributable net profit of IDR1,968.9bn, IDR2,233.1bn and IDR2,413.7bn [S0]. The revenue build assumes total sales value grows at the rate in our presales assumption, fades toward the long-run rate, and is recognised largely at handover in the year of contract, which is consistent with the accounting policy and with the size of the advance book relative to annual revenue [S3]. The development gross margin is held near the FY2025 level, fading only slowly as built products take a larger share, and the recurring margin is set at a normal range for convention and hotel operations. [S3, S0]

Our forecast now runs off the reported nine months rather than sitting below them. The company reported revenue of IDR2,560.0bn and cost of revenue of only IDR519.6bn for the first nine months of FY2026, with net profit of IDR1,820.0bn [S4]. We carry FY2026 revenue of IDR2,855.5bn and attributable profit of IDR1,968.9bn: a fourth quarter consistent with FY2025's small Q4 handover season, and a FY2026 development gross margin of 79.0% that matches the nine-month actual rather than under-cutting it [S4, S0]. The margin then fades to 67.0% by FY2030 and to the FY2025 audited level in perpetuity, because the residential and commercial-product segments earn margins far below the land lots and take share again as the land-lot pipeline is sold [S3 p.101]. Two limits on the forecast are stated plainly: the model's presales line is a handover-revenue proxy, so it cannot reproduce a IDR9,546.8bn advance book that turns only about once every four years [S3 p.400]; and the bulk commercial-land line is not evidenced by the marketing-sales KPI, which was IDR430.2bn in FY2025 and IDR448.0bn in 9M2026 [S3, S2]. We therefore treat the IDR563.1bn FY2026 marketing-sales target and the conversion of the advance book as the kill criteria for the base case, not as decoration (see the risks and monitoring sections). The revenue path without the bulk line is shown as the bear case: marketing sales alone support revenue nearer the marketing-sales figure than the revenue base, which is why the bear marks the land down as well. [S3, S2]

Working capital is the defining feature of the cash flow. Customer advances of IDR9,546.8bn at the end of FY2025 exceed annual revenue, and net working capital is negative at IDR-1,226.2bn, which means the business releases cash as it sells rather than consuming it [S3, S0]. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR1,390.4bn in FY2025 and IDR4,976.0bn in FY2024, well above reported net profit in the earlier year because of the advance inflow [S0]. Capex was IDR163.9bn, about 6.5% of revenue, and is directed at township infrastructure, NICE and the Hilton build [S0, S3]. We model capex at 6.5% of revenue before fading, which is above the historical average and reflects the hotel and convention assets still under construction. [S3]

The balance sheet is conservative in the way that matters. At the last balance-sheet date the company had cash of IDR3,121.0bn against debt of IDR249.5bn, a net cash position of IDR-2,871.6bn, and equity attributable to owners of IDR9,026.3bn with minority interests of IDR2,956.1bn [S0]. Interest income of IDR253.9bn exceeds interest expense of IDR25.6bn several times over, so the company is a net receiver of interest, not a payer, and there is no unhedged foreign-currency debt worth the name [S0]. Book value per share is Rp1,592. The minority balance is large because several project companies are only partly owned, and that is why our valuation deducts minorities from RNAV. [S0, S3]

The tax line is the main earnings-quality question. The effective tax charge was IDR49.1bn on pre-tax profit of IDR1,516.4bn, an effective rate far below the statutory rate, and the prior year was lower still [S0]. That is consistent with the treatment of land and building disposals under the final tax regime and with the mix of income, but it means the earnings are taxed more lightly than those of a conventional developer, and a change in the tax treatment would hit the net line disproportionately. We model 3.2%, which allows for some normalisation without ignoring the reported history. [S0]

On capital allocation, the company paid a dividend of IDR650.0bn before the listing, more than the attributable profit of IDR578.5bn in that year, and has paid Rp5 per share in each year since, a payout of 2.1% [S0]. The stated policy allows up to a maximum share of retained earnings after the mandatory reserve, but the actual distribution is far below that ceiling, so the dividend is not a support to the valuation [S3]. The listing proceeds were used mainly to acquire NICE and to increase stakes in project companies, which is a reasonable use of growth capital for a developer at this stage. [S3]

On earnings quality, three flags are worth stating. First, revenue is recognised at handover and the cash arrived earlier, so a slowdown in new sales shows up in marketing sales long before it shows up in revenue; that is a timing risk rather than an accounting abuse [S3]. Second, the gross margin is high because the product is land, and margins should compress as built products and hotel operations grow; our forecast assumes that compression is slow [S0]. Third, related-party balances disclosed at the balance-sheet date are small, with no trade receivables from related parties remaining at the end of FY2025, but the land supply itself comes through the master plan of the parent, which is a structural rather than a balance-sheet exposure [S3]. We could not compute an accruals ratio because the archived data pack does not carry an operating cash-flow line for the full history; we report that as a gap rather than estimate it. [S0]

We value CBDK on RNAV as the primary method, with P/E and P/BV as cross-checks. That method set fits a developer whose earnings are handover-driven and lumpy, whose asset is a land bank carried at historical cost, and whose recurring income is still too small to support a cash-flow valuation on its own. The property method card is explicit that Indonesian developers trade at persistent discounts to appraised net asset value and that the trade is band mean-reversion rather than full convergence, so the target is RNAV less a stated discount, not RNAV itself. [S0]

Our cost of equity is 11.9% and our weighted average cost of capital is 11.9%, built from a risk-free rate of 7.4%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, a country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 0.90 and a marginal tax rate of 22.0% [S0]. The debt weight is small because the company is in net cash, so the cost of equity and the cost of capital are close. We use the cost of equity to roll the valuation forward one year and to discount the dividend, which is the convention in the model. [S0]

The RNAV starts from the audited inventory, and it marks the whole of it, not one line of it. Land sits on two balance-sheet lines: current inventory of IDR6,909.5bn over 3,678,961 m2 of titled land and buildings, and non-current undeveloped land of IDR6,910.8bn over 3,341,874 m2 [S3 p.393-394], which together are the 702 ha the annual report reports. We mark it just below book: a modest uplift on the portion in production, where the audited annual margin and the much higher reported nine-month margin show sale prices above cost, and a haircut on the raw land at the tight end of the method card's band because it sits inside a township whose infrastructure is being built [S3 p.101, S4]. The earlier draft claimed a multiple of book by comparing the land value with the current-inventory line alone and ignoring the non-current undeveloped land; that was wrong, and the mark is now essentially at book.

Three items are handled explicitly. First, the IDR9,546.8bn advance book [S3 p.400] is deducted: the land value covers the same unsold pool the audited inventory covers, and the cash for units already contracted has already been received and spent, so carrying the land at value without the advance liability would count the same land twice. Second, the investment properties are carried at their audited book of IDR2,562.0bn - NICE, Menara Syariah and the Hilton PIK Dua under construction - rather than the small cap-rate value shown in the valuation table, because the method card requires a development asset to be worth at least its sunk cost until a sourced project value exists [S3 p.352]. Third, the model has no advance line, so the deduction and the property book are applied inside the land contribution in our parameters, which is why the parameter sits below the land value itself.

The RNAV per share before the 40.0% discount is set out in the valuation table, and the discounted value the method carries is Rp927 per share. It reconciles to audited equity attributable of IDR9,026.3bn plus the land revaluation from book to our mark: nothing is counted twice, and no value is credited for the unrecognised margin locked in the advance book - that margin is the upside to the call, not its base. The company discloses no independent appraisal of the land, only a fairness opinion on an affiliate transaction, which is why we mark it off the book rather than off a promoter net asset value. [S3]

The P/E cross-check gives Rp3,039 per share, applying a peer median multiple of 12.6x to FY2025 attributable profit of IDR1,360.0bn [S0]. It is far above the RNAV, and we discount it heavily for three reasons: it capitalises a peak-margin year in which the product mix was almost entirely raw land; the peer median is pulled up by township and land-bank names whose multiples reflect their own option value; and a P/E on handover earnings says nothing about the land still to be sold or about the advance book that is funding the handovers. We keep a 20% weight because it is the only method that captures the earnings the company is actually delivering and because it is what keeps the call honest - the stock is not expensive on earnings - but we do not let it drive the target. [S0]

The P/BV cross-check gives Rp1,374 per share, applying the peer median of 0.7x to book value at the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date shown in the valuation table - the same book and the same date the leg itself uses, and the same date as the net cash in the RNAV [S0]. On that book the shares trade at 1.5x P/BV against the peer median, a premium of more than double, rather than the larger premium claimed when the market was measured against stale FY2025 book. The premium can only be justified if the land is worth well above book; our RNAV says it is worth about book, and on FY2026 earnings the shares are at 8.3x P/E, at or below the peer median of 12.6x, because this is a high-margin handover year. The two multiples point in opposite directions, and that tension is the call: cheap on a peak-margin P/E, expensive on the asset that produces it. [S0]

Blending the three methods at the stated weights gives a value of Rp1,438 today, which we roll forward at the cost of equity and reduce by the next-twelve-month dividend of Rp35 to reach the base target of Rp1,575 [S0]. The probability-weighted target is Rp1,582 and, with no liquidity discount applied, the final target is Rp1,582. The weighted figure now sits below the base because the bear case shocks the land value as well as the discount and the sales growth, so the tails are no longer a rounding error. [S0]

The sensitivity table shows how little the target moves for plausible changes in sales growth and how much it moves for the two asset-side judgements: the RNAV discount and the land mark. A shift of ten percentage points in the RNAV discount moves the value by roughly the discount times the RNAV weight, and the land mark moves it in proportion, which is why we now shock both. We use a 40.0% discount, at the tight end of the persistent range for the sector, because the company is in net cash and its advances fund the township; a wider discount, closer to the middle of the band, would take the target materially lower. The allocation of the two layers is deliberate: the land is marked once, at about audited book, and the discount is the trading band applied to it, not a second haircut on the same assets. [S0]

What does the price imply? At Rp2,900, the market is valuing the equity above the undiscounted RNAV per share set out in the valuation table, so the implied discount is negative: investors are paying a premium to the audited value of the land, less the cash already received against it, rather than the discount to RNAV at which IDX township developers normally trade. A reverse DCF is not available because the price sits outside the range the model can bracket with plausible growth assumptions, so we express the implied view through the multiple instead: at 8.3x P/E and 1.5x P/BV, with a dividend yield of 1.2%, the shares are priced for the successful execution of the township, not for the current sales run-rate. [S0, S3]

The gap between the methods is the investment debate in one line. RNAV says the asset is worth less than the price; P/E says the earnings are worth about the price; P/BV says the book is worth much less than the price. We weight RNAV because the asset is the business, and we treat the P/E support as evidence that the market is not irrational, merely early. [S0]

The largest downside risk is that commercial plot demand stays weak. Marketing sales of IDR430.2bn in FY2025 met only part of the target the company had set, and the FY2026 target of IDR563.1bn is still small relative to the revenue base [S3]. If corporate buyers continue to wait, the advance book unwinds without replacement, revenue steps down after the backlog, and the premium multiple of the market compresses toward the sector. We put a high likelihood on continued weak plot demand and a high impact on the multiple, which is why the base case already sits below the market price. [S3, S4]

The second risk is valuation risk rather than operating risk. At 1.5x P/BV on the 30 June 2026 book the shares carry a premium of more than double the peer median, and premiums of that kind are vulnerable to a change in sentiment about the township or the group [S0]. We do not use the past share price as a valuation input: a fall from a post-listing high tells us what the market once believed, not what the asset is worth, and the call rests on the RNAV and the multiple rather than on the drawdown. The risk that the market re-rates the stock upward on a single bulk transaction is real and is captured in the bull case. [S0]

The third risk is concentration on the controlling shareholder and the master plan of the parent. Land supply, access, amenities and the sequencing of development all depend on Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua and the wider group, and the capital needs of the parent could affect how the listed subsidiary is managed [S3]. A related-party land purchase on terms that favour the parent, or a rights issue to fund township infrastructure, would be value-destructive for minority holders even if it were fully disclosed. [S3]

The fourth risk is execution on the recurring-income assets. NICE is operating and has an events calendar, and the Hilton is targeted for the second half of 2027, but neither has a disclosed segment profit, so the returns on the capital sunk into them are unproven [S3, S2]. If the hotel opens late or the convention centre fails to sustain occupancy, the recurring income that we value at a cap rate of 8.5% is worth less than we assume, and the interest-coverage cushion the assets are meant to provide never materialises. [S3]

The fifth risk is policy and macro. A reversal of the property incentives, a rise in policy rates, or a rupiah shock would hit buyer confidence and the capitalisation rate at the same time [S3]. The company has no material foreign-currency debt, so this is a demand and valuation risk rather than a solvency risk, but it is the channel through which a bad macro year becomes a bad equity year. [S0, S3]

Liquidity and governance risks are moderate. The free float is 11.9%, the controlling shareholder holds 88.6%, and three-month average daily turnover is thin for institutional positions rather than deep [S0]. We do not quote a turnover figure in trillions: the model carries the daily value in rupiah and the earlier draft mis-scaled it by a factor of a thousand. A small float amplifies moves in both directions and limits the weight any large fund can take, which is why we apply no liquidity discount but treat position size as a constraint. [S0]

Our scenarios are mirrored and they now shock the dominant term. The bear case applies the land-value shock, adds a negative shock to sales growth and widens the RNAV discount; the bull case applies the land-value shock in the opposite direction and does the same to growth and the discount by the same amounts, with probabilities of one half for the base case and one quarter each for the tails [S0]. The bear value is Rp1,407 and the bull value is Rp1,770, against a base of Rp1,575. The range brackets the land value rather than only the discount, which is what the previous draft failed to do: the trigger for the bear land shock is a marketing-sales print below the FY2025 level for successive quarters, or a related-party land transaction struck at a discount to carrying value. [S0, S3]

The signposts that would change our view are specific and dated. A bulk commercial land transaction at or above the FY2024 scale, an independent appraisal supporting a land value above our parameter, marketing sales running ahead of the IDR563.1bn target for two consecutive quarters, a dividend increase toward the stated policy ceiling, or the Hilton opening on time and letting at expected rates would all push us toward a higher rating [S3, S2]. On the other side, the kill threshold for the base case is marketing sales below the FY2025 level of IDR430.2bn for two consecutive quarters, or advance-book conversion slowing below its current pace, either of which would confirm that revenue is borrowing from a shrinking backlog rather than selling into demand. [S3, S2]

Ownership is concentrated and the control chain is disclosed. PT Pantai Indah Kapuk Dua is the controlling shareholder with a large majority of the shares, the public holds the remainder, and the President Commissioner, Richard Halim Kusuma, is named as the ultimate beneficial owner [S3]. The company is described in the press as a joint venture of the Agung Sedayu group and the Salim group, which means the ultimate controllers are well-known Indonesian business families with a long record of listed vehicles [S4, S2]. The free float is 11.9% and insider ownership is 88.6%, so minority holders have limited influence and the stock is exposed to supply from a small pool. [S0]

The board and management are aligned with the controlling group rather than independent of it. The President Director, Steven Kusumo, speaks for the company in the press, and the President Commissioner is the disclosed beneficial owner [S2, S3]. Neither the commissioners nor the directors held shares in the company directly at the end of FY2025, according to the annual report, which is unusual for a newly listed company and means the economic interest of management runs through the group rather than through direct equity [S3]. We treat that as a governance consideration, not a red flag on its own. [S3]

Related-party dealings are disclosed and material enough to quantify rather than dismiss. The 2025 capital increases into MAS and CGIC were purchases of additional stakes from related parties, disclosed in the subsidiaries note and funded largely from listing proceeds [S3 p.363]; on the disclosed amounts they are among the largest uses of the IPO money and a large share of attributable equity. We classify them as structure-class, not manipulation-class: they are disclosed and fairness-reviewed, but minority holders paid for stakes in affiliates at prices we cannot independently test. Advances from customers include balances owed by related parties [S3 p.400], which we classify as optics-class - disclosed and reviewed as arm's-length, but a related-party share of the advance book leaves the sales run-rate less independently verifiable than a third-party book would be. Trade receivables from related parties were negligible against the IDR2,503.6bn revenue base, and the company sets out its compliance with the affiliated-transaction and conflict-of-interest rules in the annual report [S3]. The structural exposure is the land itself: the township master plan, the amenity sequencing and the land supply sit with the parent, so the inventory of the listed entity is replenished through a related party even when no balance is outstanding at the reporting date. [S3]

We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares, no special-monitoring-board status or special notation, and no auditor downgrade. The FY2024 accounts were audited by KAP Johan Malonda Mustika & Rekan with an unqualified opinion [S3]. The audit relationship is not with a top-tier international network, which is common for mid-cap Indonesian developers but is a factor to monitor if the company grows. On the structure screens in our governance method card, the item that stands out is the pre-listing dividend of IDR650.0bn, which exceeded that year's attributable profit of IDR578.5bn and transferred cash to the then-owners before the public became shareholders [S0]. That is a distribution decision, fully disclosed, but it is the kind of capital allocation that minority holders should remember when the company asks for capital later. [S0]

The dividend record since listing is modest. The company pays Rp5 per share, a payout of 2.1%, against a stated policy that allows a much higher share of retained earnings after the mandatory reserve [S3, S0]. We model a higher payout than the historical one but still well below the policy ceiling, because the company has no commitment and its capital needs are real. [S0]

On ESG, the exposures are those of a coastal township developer: land reclamation and drainage, flood management, permits and environmental compliance, and the social impact of reshaping the area. The annual report describes water-management and flood-control work as part of the ecosystem preservation of the township, and the company frames its social programme around local economic participation [S3]. We have no independent environmental assessment, so we treat these as management claims rather than verified outcomes. The governance overlay that matters most for valuation is not the environmental record but the related-party land pipeline, and that is where diligence should concentrate. [S3]

The dated catalysts are few, which is itself a feature of a single-township developer. The Hilton PIK Dua is targeted to open in the second half of 2027, and a successful opening would convert construction spending into recurring income and give the market a second earnings stream to value [S2]. The FY2026 audited results and the dividend decision at the annual meeting in the first half of 2027 will show whether the profit run-rate of the first nine months held through the fourth quarter, which is the single most important test of our FY2026 forecast [S4, S3]. Full-year marketing sales against the IDR563.1bn target will be reported with the results and is the KPI that leads revenue by a year or more; a print below the FY2025 level of IDR430.2bn for two consecutive quarters is our kill criterion for the base case. [S3]

The event we would watch most closely is a bulk commercial land transaction. The FY2024 marketing-sales figure of IDR2,120.0bn, of which IDR1,488.9bn was commercial land lots against IDR343.5bn in FY2025, shows that a single transaction can change the sales profile of a year, and a repeat at that scale would validate the land value, support the advance book and force us to revisit the base case [S3, S5]. We would also watch the pace of third-party infrastructure in the district, since bank buildings, the Beachwalk lifestyle centre and the toll connection are the evidence that the township is becoming a place businesses want to be [S2].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are marketing sales and its mix between land plots and built products; the customer-advance balance and its current portion, as the best guide to revenue conversion; the development gross margin, as the signal of mix shift; capex on the hotel and convention assets; the recurring-revenue line and any segment disclosure for NICE; the dividend and payout; and the discount to RNAV implied by the share price. [S3, S0]

On our numbers, the stock is a SELL because the price already discounts a successful township, and the evidence so far is a company selling plots at a fraction of the pace needed to justify it. We would revisit that view on a bulk transaction, an appraisal, or two quarters of marketing sales above target, and we would add to it on a related-party land deal, a delayed hotel or a further decline in plot demand. [S0, S3]

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for CBDK.JK

S2.title: Marketing Sales CBDK Tembus Rp 448 Miliar, Ditopang Kaveling Komersial

S4.title: CBDK, Emiten Properti Kongsi Aguan dan Grup Salim, Cetak Laba Rp 1,82 Triliun

bear.narrative: Plot demand stays at the 2025 trough, the advance book converts more slowly than we assume, handovers slip, and a land-price correction takes 15% off the carried land value as the township discount widens and rates stay high.

bull.narrative: Rate cuts and the VAT exemption revive plot demand, marketing sales beat the IDR 563bn target, a bulk commercial land transaction lands at FY2024 scale, NICE and Hilton open on time, land values are marked 15% higher and the discount narrows toward the tight end of the band.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs presales growth and RNAV discount

assumptions.label: Presales growth
assumptions.basis: Contracted sales value grows 20% in FY2026: 9M2026 marketing sales of IDR 448bn are up about 40% yoy and the company's own FY2026 target is IDR 563bn, 31% above FY2025 [S2, S3 p.121], while FY2025 new contracted value derived from the advance movement was IDR 2,113.8bn (revenue 2,503.6 plus the 389.7bn fall in advances) [S3 p.400]. We do not extrapolate the 31% target growth into the bulk line; we take 20% for one year, then 8%, 6%, 5% and 4% as the marketed pipeline caps intake and the advance book unwinds. This is the most likely path, not a haircut: FY2024 marketing sales of IDR 2,114.6bn [S3 p.21] show the bulk commercial-land line can run at several times the 2025 figure when a large transaction lands.

assumptions.label: Share of presales recognised in the same year
assumptions.basis: Reconciled to the advance movement rather than asserted. FY2025 revenue of IDR 2,503.6bn plus the IDR 389.7bn fall in advances (9,936.6 to 9,546.8) implies IDR 2,113.8bn of new contracted value in the year [S3 p.400], and revenue equals 25.7% of the average advance book, i.e. the book turns about once every four years because most of it is multi-year staged bulk-land handover. The template carries a single one-year lag, so 60% in-year and 40% next year is the closest match that does not front-load revenue; section 3 discloses that the model cannot reproduce a 3.8x advance book and that conversion of the book is a monitored KPI with a kill threshold.

assumptions.label: Recurring revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Rental income was only IDR 35.5bn in FY2025 [S3 p.410] but NICE (acquired January 2025) and Hilton PIK2 (acquired March 2025, opening 2027 [S3 p.23]) add MICE and hotel capacity, so recurring revenue compounds from a small base before fading to 6% long run.

assumptions.label: Development gross margin
assumptions.basis: Carried at the reported level and faded, not cut to a guess. 9M2026 gross profit was IDR 2,030bn on revenue of IDR 2,560bn, a 79.3% margin, because commercial land lots are about 85% of presales and carry almost no construction cost [S4, S2]; FY2025 was 66% and 9M2025 69% [S3 p.410, S4]. We hold FY2026 at 79% and fade to 66% by FY2030 - the FY2025 audited level - as built products take share again (residential segment margin 41.1%, commercial products 57.3% [S3 p.101]).

assumptions.label: Recurring gross margin
assumptions.basis: Rental and MICE gross margin of 55%, a normal range for convention and hotel operations in Indonesia; no segment profitability is disclosed for NICE or Hilton yet, so this is an assumption stated as such. The cap-rate value is a cross-check only: the assets are carried at audited book (IDR 2,562.0bn) in the land-and-property contribution because NOI has barely started.

assumptions.label: Cap rate for investment property (RNAV)
assumptions.basis: 8.5% cap rate for the recurring-income assets (NICE convention centre, Hilton PIK2, Menara Syariah east tower let at IDR 175,000/sqm [S3 p.100]). Indonesian prime retail/office assets clear at 7.5-9.0%; we sit at the wide end because the assets are in a township still under construction. The cap-rate value is a cross-check only: the RNAV carries the assets at book (sunk cost), as the method card requires until a project value can be sourced.

assumptions.label: Target discount to RNAV
assumptions.basis: IDX township developers trade at a persistent 40-70% discount to RNAV (property method card and the comparable band tabulated in section 4). We use the tight end, 40%, because CBDK is in net cash, has no USD debt, and its advances fund the township. A 40% discount to an RNAV already struck at 0.95x audited book is one layer of caution, not two.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2023A-FY2025A average of 7.8% of revenue; SG&A was IDR 221.8bn on IDR 2,503.6bn in FY2025 [S0] and the cost base is largely fixed, so it should not fall as revenue grows.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default average of FY2023A-FY2025A (div(da, revenue))

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was IDR 163.9bn, 6.5% of revenue [S0]; the Hilton PIK2 build and NICE fit-out keep capex at that 6.5% for FY2026-27 before fading to 6.0%, rather than the 7.0% used before, which was above the last actual without a source.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital is negative because customer advances fund the development: net working capital was -IDR 1,226bn in FY2025 on IDR 9.5trn of advances [S0]. We hold NWC at -45% of revenue rather than the positive default, which would wrongly assume the business is cash-hungry.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax was IDR 49.1bn on PBT of IDR 1,516.4bn, a 3.2% effective rate, and FY2024 was 1.3% [S0]; 9M2026 shows a nil tax charge [S0]. We use 3.2%, the last actual, rather than a 5% normalisation nobody has evidenced.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default average of FY2023A-FY2025A (div(interest_expense, debt[-1]))

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default average of FY2023A-FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: no new net debt assumed; the company is in net cash (IDR 3.1trn cash against IDR 0.2trn debt)

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 7.0% of FY2025 net profit (IDR 103.1bn of IDR 1,467.3bn [S0]); the capital increases into MAS (55.89% to 77.35%) and CGIC (to 78.46%) in 2025 [S3 p.7] raise parent ownership, so we use 8% and hold it.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: DPS has been IDR 5 in each of FY2024 and FY2025 [S0], about 2-3% of EPS; we model 10% of earnings, above the reported record but short of any commitment the company has not made.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: no new issuance assumed; 5,668.9m shares outstanding after the January 2025 corporate action

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5.0% nominal terminal growth: land prices in a Jakarta satellite township grow with nominal GDP (about 8.6% in the house macro deck) but we take roughly half of it, above CPI and above the previous unsourced 4%. It applies only to the cross-check DCF, not to the RNAV.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E gross profit of 1,789bn (revenue 2,795.4bn x 64% margin) is below the 2,030bn gross profit already reported for 9M2026, and FY2026E attributable profit of 1,535.2bn is below the 1,820bn reported for 9M2026 [S4]. 9M2025 net profit of 1,310bn was 89% of FY2025's 1,467bn, so the same seasonality implies FY2026 net profit of ~1,950-2,040bn. A fourth quarter with negative gross profit is not the most-likely case and is not justified anywhere.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt FY2026 from the nine-month actuals: revenue, cost of revenue and net profit for 9M2026 are now facts F17, F27 and F18, and FY2026 carries the reported 79pc development margin instead of 64pc, with a Q4 consistent with the small FY2025 handover quarter. FY2026 attributable profit is now above the 9M figure; the P/E, roll-forward and target were re-run.

challenges.challenge: The landbank_value of 13,000bn is described as roughly twice the audited inventory value of 6,909.5bn. S3 p.352 shows 6,909.5bn is only the current inventory line and that non-current undeveloped land is a further 6,910.8bn, for total land inventory of 13,820bn (368 ha under development plus 334 ha undeveloped, S3 p.244). The land is therefore marked at 0.94x book, not 1.9x, and the section 1 and 4 statements that the 1.9x already contains the raw-land haircut and that inventory is a fraction of the revenue the area has generated are both contradicted by the filing.
challenges.answer: Land is marked against the two audited inventory lines, current 6,909.5bn over 3,678,961 m2 and non-current undeveloped 6,910.8bn over 3,341,874 m2, i.e. 13,820.4bn for 702 ha, with a modest uplift on land in production and a raw-land haircut at the tight end of the method card band. The mark is now about book, not 1.9x; the 1.9x claim compared the value with the current-inventory line alone and is removed from sections 1 and 4.

challenges.challenge: The RNAV bridge deducts net debt, deducts minorities and adds associates but deducts no customer advances, although the property method card requires RNAV less advances. Advances were 9,546.8bn at FY2025, of which 8,410.8bn current [S3 p.400]. The 13,000bn land value covers roughly 390-433 ha at the stated 3.0m per sqm ASP, which necessarily includes land already sold against those advances, so the RNAV counts the same land twice: once as inventory value and once as cash already received.
challenges.answer: The 9,546.8bn advance book is deducted explicitly inside the land contribution because the engine RNAV build has no advance line; the reduction is disclosed in section 4. RNAV now reconciles to audited equity attributable of 9,026.3bn plus the land revaluation, so land already sold is not counted twice and no value is credited for the unrecognised margin on the advance book.

challenges.challenge: The report argues margins must compress, but the actuals show the opposite: 9M2026 gross profit of 2,030bn on revenue of 2,560bn is a 79.3% margin versus 66% in FY2025 and 64% in the model, because commercial land lots are 85% of presales [S2]. The higher-margin mix is accelerating, not fading, and the report never argues why that reverses.
challenges.answer: The 9M2026 gross margin of 79.3pc (gross profit 2,030bn on revenue 2,560bn, cost of revenue 519.6bn) is carried in FY2026, and the fade is sourced: to the FY2025 audited 66pc by FY2030 as built products take share, with residential and commercial-product segments earning far lower margins than land lots.

challenges.challenge: The recurring arm is assigned 419bn, which is exactly rental revenue of 35.5bn capitalised at 8.5% - gross rent treated as net operating income - while NICE (acquired January 2025 with IPO proceeds) and the Hilton PIK2 under construction are carried on the balance sheet and given no separate value. The method card requires a development asset to be worth at least its sourced sunk capex until a sourced project value exists.
challenges.answer: Investment properties are carried at audited book of 2,562.0bn (NICE, Menara Syariah, Hilton PIK Dua), not the 419bn the 8.5pc cap rate gives on gross rent; the excess is added inside the land contribution and the cap-rate value is kept only as a cross-check, so both assets are valued at least at sunk cost.

challenges.challenge: The RNAV is 60% of the blend, yet no scenario shocks land value or ASP: the bear only adds 10 points to the discount and cuts presales growth by 8 points, giving 1,815, an 8.5% gap to base that is still above the report's own RNAV. The report admits it has not modelled a land-price shock, which leaves the dominant term untested and makes the probability weighting add nothing to the target.
challenges.answer: Both scenarios now shock the land value through p.landbank_value, mirrored: bear 0.85x with a wider discount and slower sales, bull 1.15x with the reverse. The bear trigger is dated: marketing sales below the FY2025 level for successive quarters, or a related-party land sale below carrying value.

challenges.challenge: Governance risk is understated. Note 11 [S3 p.400] shows 570.0bn of sales advances are from related parties, 23% of FY2025 revenue, not negligible. The 2025 capital increases into MAS (2.63trn) and CGIC (0.98trn) were related-party purchases totalling 3.6trn, about 34% of attributable equity, funded largely from listing proceeds. None of this is quantified as related-party flow against revenue or equity.
challenges.answer: Quantified and classified in section 6: the 2025 MAS and CGIC capital increases were related-party purchases funded largely from listing proceeds and are a structure-class flag; related-party customer advances are an optics-class flag; trade receivables from related parties were negligible against revenue. Pledged shares, notation and auditor checks remain clean.

challenges.challenge: The assumption that 80% of each year's contracted value is recognised in the year of contract is inconsistent with the advance book by an order of magnitude: under it the unrecognised balance should be about 20% of one year of contracts, around 0.5-0.6trn, whereas the reported balance is 9,546.8bn, roughly 3.8x annual revenue and implying a conversion rate near 25% a year.
challenges.answer: recog_current cut from 80pc to 60pc and reconciled to the advance movement: revenue 2,503.6bn plus the 389.7bn fall in advances implies 2,113.8bn of new contracts, and the book turns about once every four years. Section 3 states the single-lag limit of the template and adds advance conversion as a monitored KPI.

challenges.challenge: The P/BV argument is internally inconsistent: the P/BV leg applies a 0.73 peer multiple to 1H2026 book (10,566.1bn over 5,643m shares, 1,872 per share, giving 1,374) while the surrounding text measures the market at 1.8x using stale FY2025 book of 1,592 per share. On the book the leg actually uses, the shares trade at 1.55x, not 1.8x, and the premium to the peer median is 111%, not 145%.
challenges.answer: One book and one date throughout: the P/BV leg book of 10,566.1bn at 30 June 2026 is now the book used in the text, and the market multiple on that basis is 1.56x, not 1.8x, with the premium described as more than double rather than 145pc. The FY2025 book reference was removed.

challenges.challenge: Conservatism is stacked without sources in a way that moves the target: land at 0.94x audited book and then a further 40% RNAV discount applies the same caution twice; terminal growth of 4% sits against a nominal GDP path of about 8.6% from the house deck; capex is 7.0% against a 6.5% actual; the tax rate is 5% against a 3.2% effective rate; and the Hilton is worth zero. No single item is fatal but together they bias the base case low, and only the payout ratio (10% against 2.1% actual) points the other way.
challenges.answer: Each departure sourced or removed: land marked once at about book with a raw-land haircut and the 40pc discount read as the trading band, not a second haircut; terminal growth raised to 5pc against an 8.6pc nominal GDP path; capex cut to the 6.5pc last actual; tax cut to the 3.2pc effective rate; Hilton carried at book, not zero.

challenges.challenge: The property method card's output contract requires a named discount catalyst with a date and the name's own five-year discount band. The report has neither: own history is described as unavailable because the company listed in January 2025, and the SELL depends on the shares reverting from a negative implied discount to a 40% RNAV discount with no dated catalyst. A call whose value is set by a mean-reversion with no observable band is not actionable.
challenges.answer: A dated catalyst is named: the Hilton PIK Dua opening targeted for the second half of 2027, the FY2026 results in the first half of 2027 and the FY2026 marketing-sales print against the 563bn target. The 40pc discount is the tight end of the 40-70pc band for IDX township developers on the property method card, and section 4 states the band.

challenges.challenge: The revenue path requires about 2.8trn of sales value in FY2026 rising to 4.4trn by FY2035, while the only disclosed sales KPI is marketing sales of 430.2bn in FY2025, 448bn in 9M2026 and a 2026 target of 563bn [S3 p.46, S2]. The model therefore assumes roughly 2.2trn a year of bulk land transactions that the KPI does not evidence, and there is no marketing-sales kill criterion as the method card requires.
challenges.answer: The bulk line is explicit and sourced: FY2025 new contracted value of 2,113.8bn is derived from the advance movement, and FY2024 marketing sales of 2,114.6bn included 1,488.9bn of commercial land lots against 343.5bn in FY2025. The marketing-sales target and the conversion rate are stated kill criteria, and the path without the bulk line is the bear case.

challenges.challenge: Two numbers in the liquidity paragraph cannot be verified or are wrong by a factor of a thousand: three-month average daily turnover is stated as IDR9,947,642.95tn when the model carries 9,947,642,952 rupiah, about 9.95bn a day; and the Rp9,425 high used to support the de-rating appears in no source in the packet and is not in the report source.
challenges.answer: The turnover figure is removed rather than mis-scaled: section 5 now says turnover is thin for institutional positions and notes the previous figure was wrong by a factor of a thousand. The Rp9,425 high is deleted and no past price is used as evidence anywhere.

challenges.challenge: The drawdown from Rp9,425 to Rp2,900 is used as evidence that part of the de-rating has happened, but a past price is not a valuation input and the report offers no view on why the market paid 9,425 or what changed. Combined with a 12.1x P/E framed as expensive when the peer median in the same model is 12.6x, the tone leans bearish beyond what the numbers support.
challenges.answer: The price-history argument is removed and the multiple stated honestly: the shares trade at 10.7x FY2026E P/E against a peer median of 12.6x, i.e. at or below the peer median on the model own set, while P/BV is above it. The tension is presented as the call rather than as evidence of over-valuation.

missing_bull_case.note: The strongest bull evidence is absent: 9M2026 gross margin was 79.3% (GP 2,030 on revenue 2,560 [S4]) versus 64% in the model, and forward P/E on a realistic FY2026 profit is ~8.6x, not the 12.1x trailing multiple the report uses to argue the shares are priced for perfection.

missing_bear_case.note: No scenario shocks land value, the term that carries 60% of the blend, so the bear case (1,815) is only 8.5% below base and still above the RNAV the report itself derives; and related-party flows (570bn of related-party sales advances, 3.6trn of related-party stake purchases) are described as negligible.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E GP of 1,789bn (2,795.4 x 64%) is below the 2,030bn already booked in 9M2026 and FY2026E NP of 1,535bn is below the 1,820bn 9M actual; 9M2025 was 89% of FY2025 NP, implying FY2026 NP of ~1,950-2,040bn. recog_current of 80% is also inconsistent with a 9,546.8bn advance book that equals 3.8x revenue.

evidence_and_citations.note: The landbank basis is misdescribed against the filing (6,909.5bn is current inventory only; non-current undeveloped land is a further 6,910.8bn, S3 p.352/393), the 1.8x P/BV claim uses stale FY2025 book while the P/BV leg uses 1H2026 book (1.55x), and the Rp9,425 high and IDR9,947,642.95tn turnover are unsourced or unit-wrong.

valuation_method_fit.note: The RNAV build deducts net debt, deducts minorities and adds associates but never deducts customer advances, which the property method card explicitly requires, and assigns only 419bn to the entire recurring arm while omitting other investments and prepaid tax; no dated discount catalyst or own-history discount band is given as the card's output contract requires.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the evidence in three places: it calls the market priced above undiscounted RNAV when that RNAV is inflated by omitted advance liabilities, it leans on the 9,425-to-2,900 drawdown as valuation support, and it calls the earnings expensive on a trailing multiple that the company's own 9M run-rate already halves.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Peers CTRA and PWON are BUY on the same township method, and the published CTRA thesis is land at cost net of advances; CBDK's model does the opposite on both counts without reconciling why one industry yields BUY for peers and SELL here. The house macro deck is AVOID on INDO property and the report never states that it agrees.

conservatism_audit.note: Stacked and unsourced: land at 0.94x audited book then a further 40% RNAV discount (the same caution twice), terminal growth 4% against 8.6% nominal GDP, capex 7.0% against 6.5% actual, tax 5% against 3.2% actual, and Hilton PIK2 (opening 2H2027) valued at zero. Some of these move value; together they bias the base case low.

calibration.note: The engine shows no BLOCK flags and a FY2025 EBITDA-margin gap of only -1.22pp, so mechanical calibration passes. The substantive calibration failure is that FY+1 does not reproduce the reported 9M2026 actuals at all: revenue is fine at 2,795 vs 2,560, but gross profit and net profit are both below nine months of actuals.

signoff.notes: Summary and section 4 wording checked against the model: price Rp2,900 is above both the post-discount RNAV (Rp927) and the implied pre-discount RNAV (about Rp1,545), so the QC NOTE is a phrasing nit, not a contradiction. RNAV 927 primary at 60% weight; P/E 3,039 and P/B 1,374 disclosed as +228%/+48% to RNAV with reasons; target 1,582 gives SELL -44%. QC PASS, no owed items.

bias.note: FY2026 sits on 9M2026 actuals: revenue 2,855.5 vs 9M 2,550 (+11% yoy, S4), implying Q4 of 305bn against Q4-2025 of 207bn (FY2025 2,503.6 less 9M2025 2,297) - normal seasonality, not an unsourced decline; NP 1,968.9 > 9M 1,820. FY2026 79.3% gross margin is actual, the fade to 66% is audited FY2025 [S3 p.410]. Scenarios mirrored (-8/+8pp presales, land x0.85/1.15, discount +/-10pp), base 50%. No stacked conservatism found.

findings.finding: Summary says the price is above the undiscounted RNAV per share; RNAV 8,714.5 / 5,643m shares = Rp1,544 before the 40% discount, so the statement is true but reads ambiguously.
Assumption text cites 5,668.9m shares while the engine uses 5,643m (RNAV Rp1,544 per share); 0.5% difference, no target impact.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves +13.5pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The step is the reported mix, not a forecast hope: 9M2026 gross profit of IDR 2,030bn on revenue of IDR 2,560bn is a 79.3% margin against 66% in FY2025 because commercial land lots, which carry no construction cost, are about 85% of presales [S4, S3 p.410, S2]. Holding FY2026 at the 9M2026 level is the most likely path; the fade back to 66% is sourced to the segment margins.

flags.message: a.dev_gross_margin moves -13.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The 13pp fade from FY2026E to FY2035E goes to the FY2025 audited 66% [S3 p.410], not below it: it reflects built products taking share again, with residential segment margin 41.1% and commercial products 57.3% in the FY2025 segment note [S3 p.101]. No unsourced compression below the last actual.

flags.message: expected return -44%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Two sourced drivers produce the -44%: (1) the RNAV, struck at 0.95x the audited inventory of IDR 13,820.4bn less the IDR 9,546.8bn advance book, gives a per-share value the IDR 2,900 price sits well above [S3 p.393-394, p.400]; (2) P/BV of 1.55x on audited book with marketing sales of IDR 448bn in 9M2026 against revenue of IDR 2,560bn, i.e. the P&L is running on a shrinking backlog [S2, S4].
